# Exercise 2.4 — Missing data and imputation {#sec-imputation}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## 20 minutes, in R or in Python
Pick a tab and stay in it. The two tabs are the same exercise — the same steps,
the same questions, and the same numbers apart from one place that says so.
:::

## Objectives

By the end of this exercise you will be able to:

- describe who is missing, not just how much;
- fill a missing number with a mean or median, and a missing category with its
  mode, and say what each does to the distribution;
- argue for keeping "Unknown" as a category;
- impute a value from a patient's other measurements;
- measure how wrong an imputation was, and say why it could not have been
  right.

## The scenario

`hospital_admissions.csv` holds 250 emergency and elective admissions. The aim,
eventually, is to predict length of stay — but some of the information is
missing. Creatinine results are often not back yet when an emergency patient's
record is extracted, and some patients have no recorded smoking status.

:::::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

### 1. Explore the missingness

Load the data and count what is missing.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
library(finalfit)
library(mice)

hospital <- read_csv("data/hospital_admissions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(hospital)
colSums(is.na(hospital))
```

Creatinine is missing for 42 of the 250 patients and smoking status for 32.
Before deciding what to do about that, ask *who* is missing. Compare the
patients with and without a creatinine result:

```{r}
hospital <- hospital |>
  mutate(creatinine_missing = factor(
    if_else(is.na(creatinine), "Missing", "Observed")))

hospital |>
  summary_factorlist(
    dependent   = "creatinine_missing",
    explanatory = c("admission_type", "age", "systolic_BP", "heart_rate"),
    p = TRUE
  )
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. Are the patients with missing creatinine systematically different from the
   rest? In which variable?
2. What would happen to the cohort if you simply removed every patient with a
   missing value?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Yes, and in one variable only. Emergency admissions make up 71% of the patients
with no creatinine result but 50% of those with one (p = 0.018). Age, blood
pressure and heart rate show no convincing difference.

That is worth noticing: the missingness follows *how the patient arrived*, not
what their measurements were. A comparison of the measurements alone would have
found nothing.

```{r}
complete <- hospital |> drop_na()

nrow(complete)
round(100 * mean(hospital$admission_type == "Emergency"), 1)
round(100 * mean(complete$admission_type == "Emergency"), 1)
```

Dropping incomplete rows keeps 182 of 250 — more than a quarter of the cohort
gone — and the loss is not even. Emergency admissions fall from 53.6% of the
data to 45.6%. A model fitted to what remains has been trained on a cohort that
is more elective than the hospital really is, and nothing in the output would
tell you.
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. Simple imputation

#### A number: mean and median

The simplest thing to do with a missing number is to put the column's own
average in its place.

```{r}
hospital <- hospital |>
  mutate(
    creatinine_mean   = replace_na(creatinine, mean(creatinine, na.rm = TRUE)),
    creatinine_median = replace_na(creatinine, median(creatinine, na.rm = TRUE))
  )

round(mean(hospital$creatinine, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
median(hospital$creatinine, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Now look at what that did to the distribution:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| warning: false
hospital |>
  select(observed = creatinine, `mean imputed` = creatinine_mean) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ name) +
  labs(x = "Creatinine (µmol/L)", y = "Patients")

round(sd(hospital$creatinine, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
round(sd(hospital$creatinine_mean), 1)
```

#### A category: the most common value, or an honest "Unknown"

Smoking status has three categories — Never, Former and Current — so there is
no mean to take. The usual substitute is the most frequent category. The
alternative is to say what you actually know.

```{r}
mode_smoking <- hospital |>
  filter(!is.na(smoking_status)) |>
  count(smoking_status, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(smoking_status)

hospital <- hospital |>
  mutate(
    smoking_imputed = replace_na(smoking_status, mode_smoking),
    smoking_unknown = replace_na(smoking_status, "Unknown")
  )

hospital |> count(smoking_status)
hospital |> count(smoking_imputed)
hospital |> count(smoking_unknown)
```

Before choosing between them, look at who the unknowns are:

```{r}
hospital |>
  group_by(smoking_unknown) |>
  summarise(patients = n(),
            pct_emergency = round(100 * mean(admission_type == "Emergency")))
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. What did mean imputation do to the creatinine histogram, and to its standard
   deviation?
2. What happened to the smoking-status distribution after filling with the most
   common category?
3. Would keeping "Unknown" as its own category be more appropriate here? Use
   the last table to argue it.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
**Creatinine.** Forty-two patients now sit on exactly the same value, 78.9, and
the histogram grows a spike there that no real cohort has. The standard
deviation falls from 24.4 to 22.2. Nothing was learned about those patients,
but the column now looks more consistent than the measurements ever were — and
every confidence interval computed from it afterwards will be too narrow. The
median version does the same thing at 76.

**Smoking.** "Never" was 107 of 250 patients, 42.8%. After mode imputation it
is 139, 55.6%. Thirteen percentage points of never-smokers were created by the
filling, and the other two categories did not move — the commonest group got
commoner, which is exactly the direction that hides a minority.

**Unknown.** Yes, here. The patients with no recorded smoking status are 84%
emergency admissions, against roughly half of everyone else. They are not a
random sample of the cohort: they are the people nobody had time to ask.
Relabelling all 32 of them as never-smokers erases that. Keeping `Unknown` as a
category invents nothing, and leaves a model free to learn that "not asked" is
itself informative.

The general rule: fill a category with its mode only when you believe the gaps
are scattered at random. When *who is missing* carries meaning, say so.
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. Using the other variables

Mean and median imputation give every patient the same number, whatever else is
known about them. But an 85-year-old emergency admission and a 30-year-old
elective one are unlikely to have the same creatinine. Can age, blood pressure
and heart rate do better?

`mice` fits a regression of creatinine on the other three columns, using the
patients where it was measured, and predicts it where it was not. It is
installed along with `finalfit`, so there is nothing extra to set up.

```{r}
imp <- hospital |>
  select(age, systolic_BP, heart_rate, creatinine) |>
  mice(m = 1, maxit = 1, method = "norm.predict", printFlag = FALSE)

hospital$creatinine_advanced <- complete(imp)$creatinine

sum(is.na(hospital$creatinine_advanced))
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What the three arguments mean
`m = 1` asks for one filled-in dataset. `maxit = 1` is one pass, which is all
that is needed here because only creatinine has gaps among these four columns.
`method = "norm.predict"` fills each gap with the regression's best guess.

The Python tab does the same job with scikit-learn's `IterativeImputer`. The
two are the same idea, so their answers land very close together but are not
identical.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
Two patients of the same age, with the same blood pressure and heart rate, will
be given the same imputed creatinine. Why might their real values be very
different?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Because creatinine depends on things this table does not contain: kidney
disease, muscle mass, hydration, sex, the drugs the patient is on. Two patients
who look identical on three vital signs can differ on every one of those.

The imputer can only use the columns it is given. It is not estimating the
patient's creatinine; it is reporting the average creatinine of patients who
resemble them on age, blood pressure and heart rate.
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4. The reveal: how close were we?

For 18 of the patients with no creatinine, the real measurement was kept back.
Here it is.

```{r}
creatinine_truth <- read_csv("data/creatinine_truth.csv",
                             show_col_types = FALSE)

comparison <- hospital |>
  inner_join(creatinine_truth, by = "patient_id")

comparison |>
  select(patient_id, true_creatinine,
         creatinine_mean, creatinine_median, creatinine_advanced) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1))) |>
  head(6)
```

Read across each row. The mean and median columns are one number repeated. The
last column moves with the patient — and still does not match the truth for
any of them.

Now the average size of the miss, across all 18:

```{r}
comparison |>
  summarise(
    Mean     = mean(abs(true_creatinine - creatinine_mean)),
    Median   = mean(abs(true_creatinine - creatinine_median)),
    Advanced = mean(abs(true_creatinine - creatinine_advanced))
  ) |>
  round(2)
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. Which method came closest?
2. Did the advanced method get any single patient exactly right?
3. What clinical information, missing from this table, would have helped?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
The advanced method, with an average miss of about 8.4 µmol/L against 11.4 for
the mean and 11.3 for the median. (It reads 8.45 in the R tab and 8.35 in the
Python tab, because the two packages fit the regression slightly differently.)

It got **none** of the 18 exactly right. Only 6 were within 5 µmol/L. The worst
was patient H151, imputed at about 113 against a real 92 — more than 20 out.

So using the other variables helped, by about a quarter. It did not recover the
truth, and it could not have: renal history, medication and muscle mass are the
things that move creatinine, and none of them is in the table.
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### What to take from this

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Imputation is making data up
Every value you filled in this exercise is an invention. A careful one, in the
last case, but an invention — and once it is in the column it looks exactly like
a measurement.
:::

1. **Look at who is missing before deciding what to do.** Here the gaps tracked
   emergency admission, so dropping them would have quietly changed the cohort.
2. **Simple methods distort.** The mean put 42 patients on one value and
   shrank the spread; the mode turned 43% never-smokers into 56%.
3. **Better methods are better, not right.** Using three other variables cut
   the error by about a quarter and still missed one patient by more than 20.
4. **Sometimes the honest answer is a category called Unknown.**

### Optional: multiple imputation

The `mice` package is built for something more than the single fill used above.
Its default method does not give each gap one best guess; it draws a *plausible*
value, and it is meant to be run several times, so that the spread between the
filled-in datasets shows how uncertain each value was. That is multiple
imputation, and it is the honest way to carry imputation uncertainty through to
a final result. Read more at [amices.org/mice](https://amices.org/mice/).

## Python

### 1. Explore the missingness

Load the data and count what is missing.

```{python}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

hospital = pd.read_csv("data/hospital_admissions.csv")

print(hospital.dtypes)
print(hospital.isna().sum())
```

Creatinine is missing for 42 of the 250 patients and smoking status for 32.
Before deciding what to do about that, ask *who* is missing. Compare the
patients with and without a creatinine result:

```{python}
hospital["creatinine_missing"] = np.where(
    hospital["creatinine"].isna(), "Missing", "Observed")

table = pd.crosstab(hospital["admission_type"], hospital["creatinine_missing"])
print((100 * table / table.sum()).round(1))
print("p =", round(stats.chi2_contingency(table)[1], 3), "\n")

for col in ["age", "systolic_BP", "heart_rate"]:
    missing  = hospital.loc[hospital["creatinine_missing"] == "Missing", col]
    observed = hospital.loc[hospital["creatinine_missing"] == "Observed", col]
    print(f"{col:12s} {missing.mean():6.1f} ({missing.std():.1f})   "
          f"{observed.mean():6.1f} ({observed.std():.1f})   "
          f"p = {stats.ttest_ind(missing, observed).pvalue:.3f}")
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. Are the patients with missing creatinine systematically different from the
   rest? In which variable?
2. What would happen to the cohort if you simply removed every patient with a
   missing value?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Yes, and in one variable only. Emergency admissions make up 71% of the patients
with no creatinine result but 50% of those with one (p = 0.018). Age, blood
pressure and heart rate show no convincing difference.

That is worth noticing: the missingness follows *how the patient arrived*, not
what their measurements were. A comparison of the measurements alone would have
found nothing.

```{python}
complete = hospital.dropna()

print(len(complete))
print(round(100 * (hospital["admission_type"] == "Emergency").mean(), 1))
print(round(100 * (complete["admission_type"] == "Emergency").mean(), 1))
```

Dropping incomplete rows keeps 182 of 250 — more than a quarter of the cohort
gone — and the loss is not even. Emergency admissions fall from 53.6% of the
data to 45.6%. A model fitted to what remains has been trained on a cohort that
is more elective than the hospital really is, and nothing in the output would
tell you.
:::
:::

### 2. Simple imputation

#### A number: mean and median

The simplest thing to do with a missing number is to put the column's own
average in its place.

```{python}
hospital["creatinine_mean"] = hospital["creatinine"].fillna(
    hospital["creatinine"].mean())
hospital["creatinine_median"] = hospital["creatinine"].fillna(
    hospital["creatinine"].median())

print(round(hospital["creatinine"].mean(), 1))
print(hospital["creatinine"].median())
```

Now look at what that did to the distribution:

```{python}
#| fig-height: 2.8
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 2.8), sharey=True)
axes[0].hist(hospital["creatinine_mean"], bins=30, color="steelblue")
axes[0].set_title("mean imputed")
axes[1].hist(hospital["creatinine"].dropna(), bins=30, color="steelblue")
axes[1].set_title("observed")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("Creatinine (µmol/L)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Patients")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(round(hospital["creatinine"].std(), 1))
print(round(hospital["creatinine_mean"].std(), 1))
```

#### A category: the most common value, or an honest "Unknown"

Smoking status has three categories — Never, Former and Current — so there is
no mean to take. The usual substitute is the most frequent category. The
alternative is to say what you actually know.

```{python}
mode_smoking = hospital["smoking_status"].value_counts().index[0]

hospital["smoking_imputed"] = hospital["smoking_status"].fillna(mode_smoking)
hospital["smoking_unknown"] = hospital["smoking_status"].fillna("Unknown")

print(hospital["smoking_status"].value_counts(dropna=False).sort_index())
print(hospital["smoking_imputed"].value_counts().sort_index())
print(hospital["smoking_unknown"].value_counts().sort_index())
```

Before choosing between them, look at who the unknowns are:

```{python}
print(hospital.groupby("smoking_unknown").agg(
    patients=("patient_id", "size"),
    pct_emergency=("admission_type",
                   lambda s: round(100 * (s == "Emergency").mean()))))
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. What did mean imputation do to the creatinine histogram, and to its standard
   deviation?
2. What happened to the smoking-status distribution after filling with the most
   common category?
3. Would keeping "Unknown" as its own category be more appropriate here? Use
   the last table to argue it.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
**Creatinine.** Forty-two patients now sit on exactly the same value, 78.9, and
the histogram grows a spike there that no real cohort has. The standard
deviation falls from 24.4 to 22.2. Nothing was learned about those patients,
but the column now looks more consistent than the measurements ever were — and
every confidence interval computed from it afterwards will be too narrow. The
median version does the same thing at 76.

**Smoking.** "Never" was 107 of 250 patients, 42.8%. After mode imputation it
is 139, 55.6%. Thirteen percentage points of never-smokers were created by the
filling, and the other two categories did not move — the commonest group got
commoner, which is exactly the direction that hides a minority.

**Unknown.** Yes, here. The patients with no recorded smoking status are 84%
emergency admissions, against roughly half of everyone else. They are not a
random sample of the cohort: they are the people nobody had time to ask.
Relabelling all 32 of them as never-smokers erases that. Keeping `Unknown` as a
category invents nothing, and leaves a model free to learn that "not asked" is
itself informative.

The general rule: fill a category with its mode only when you believe the gaps
are scattered at random. When *who is missing* carries meaning, say so.
:::
:::

### 3. Using the other variables

Mean and median imputation give every patient the same number, whatever else is
known about them. But an 85-year-old emergency admission and a 30-year-old
elective one are unlikely to have the same creatinine. Can age, blood pressure
and heart rate do better?

`IterativeImputer` fits a regression of creatinine on the other three columns,
using the patients where it was measured, and predicts it where it was not. It
is still marked experimental in scikit-learn, so it has to be switched on.

```{python}
from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer  # noqa: F401
from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer

features = ["age", "systolic_BP", "heart_rate", "creatinine"]

imputer = IterativeImputer(random_state=42)
hospital["creatinine_advanced"] = (
    imputer.fit_transform(hospital[features])[:, -1])

print(int(hospital["creatinine_advanced"].isna().sum()))
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The same idea in R
The R tab does this job with the `mice` package. The two are the same idea —
a regression on the other columns — so their answers land very close together
but are not identical.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
Two patients of the same age, with the same blood pressure and heart rate, will
be given the same imputed creatinine. Why might their real values be very
different?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Because creatinine depends on things this table does not contain: kidney
disease, muscle mass, hydration, sex, the drugs the patient is on. Two patients
who look identical on three vital signs can differ on every one of those.

The imputer can only use the columns it is given. It is not estimating the
patient's creatinine; it is reporting the average creatinine of patients who
resemble them on age, blood pressure and heart rate.
:::
:::

### 4. The reveal: how close were we?

For 18 of the patients with no creatinine, the real measurement was kept back.
Here it is.

```{python}
creatinine_truth = pd.read_csv("data/creatinine_truth.csv")

comparison = hospital.merge(creatinine_truth, on="patient_id")

print(comparison[["patient_id", "true_creatinine", "creatinine_mean",
                  "creatinine_median", "creatinine_advanced"]]
      .round(1).head(6).to_string(index=False))
```

Read across each row. The mean and median columns are one number repeated. The
last column moves with the patient — and still does not match the truth for
any of them.

Now the average size of the miss, across all 18:

```{python}
print({name: round(float((comparison["true_creatinine"] - comparison[col])
                         .abs().mean()), 2)
       for name, col in [("Mean", "creatinine_mean"),
                         ("Median", "creatinine_median"),
                         ("Advanced", "creatinine_advanced")]})
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. Which method came closest?
2. Did the advanced method get any single patient exactly right?
3. What clinical information, missing from this table, would have helped?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
The advanced method, with an average miss of about 8.4 µmol/L against 11.4 for
the mean and 11.3 for the median. (It reads 8.45 in the R tab and 8.35 in the
Python tab, because the two packages fit the regression slightly differently.)

It got **none** of the 18 exactly right. Only 6 were within 5 µmol/L. The worst
was patient H151, imputed at about 113 against a real 92 — more than 20 out.

So using the other variables helped, by about a quarter. It did not recover the
truth, and it could not have: renal history, medication and muscle mass are the
things that move creatinine, and none of them is in the table.
:::
:::
